\longrightarrow
N-1
\longrightarrow
N.
$$ {#eq-divisive-direction}

The two approaches therefore construct the hierarchy from opposite directions.

## Top-Down Construction

Let the complete observation set be

$$
\mathcal{S}
=
\{1,2,\ldots,N\}.
$$

The initial divisive partition is

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(1)}
=
\{\mathcal{S}\}.
$$ {#eq-divisive-initial-partition}

At each stage, one existing cluster is selected and divided into two non-empty daughter clusters.

Suppose the selected cluster is $C$. A binary split produces

$$
C_A\cup C_B=C,
$$

subject to

$$
C_A\cap C_B=\varnothing,
$$

$$
C_A\neq\varnothing,
\qquad
C_B\neq\varnothing.
$$ {#eq-divisive-binary-split}

If the current partition contains $K$ clusters,

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(K)}
=
\{C_1,\ldots,C_K\},
$$

and $C_r$ is selected for division, the next partition is

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(K+1)}
=
\left(
\mathcal{P}^{(K)}
\setminus
\{C_r\}
\right)
\cup
\{C_A,C_B\}.
$$ {#eq-divisive-partition-update}

The process continues until every observation forms its own cluster:

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(N)}
=
\big\{
\{1\},\{2\},\ldots,\{N\}
\big\}.
$$ {#eq-divisive-final-partition}

As in the agglomerative case, the complete procedure contains $N-1$ binary operations. The difference is their direction: agglomerative clustering constructs parent clusters from daughter clusters, whereas divisive clustering constructs daughter clusters from parent clusters.

The result in both cases is a nested sequence of partitions.

## The Splitting Problem

The central decision in an agglomerative algorithm is

> Which two clusters should be merged next?

The corresponding question in a divisive algorithm is more involved:

> Which existing cluster should be divided, and how should its observations be divided into two groups?

For a cluster $C$ containing $n_C$ observations, a binary split requires finding two non-empty subsets $C_A$ and $C_B$ satisfying

$$
C_A\cup C_B=C
$$

and

$$
C_A\cap C_B=\varnothing.
$$

The number of distinct unordered non-trivial binary partitions of $C$ is

$$
2^{n_C-1}-1.
$$ {#eq-number-binary-splits}

To derive this result, observe that each of the $n_C$ observations can initially be assigned to either of two groups, giving

$$
2^{n_C}
$$

possible assignments.

Two assignments place all observations in the same group and therefore do not define a non-trivial split. This leaves

$$
2^{n_C}-2
$$

assignments.

Finally, the division

$$
(C_A,C_B)
$$

represents the same unordered split as

$$
(C_B,C_A),
$$

so the count must be divided by two:

$$
\frac{2^{n_C}-2}{2}
=
2^{n_C-1}-1.
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\text{number of non-trivial binary splits}
=
2^{n_C-1}-1
}
$$

and exhaustive evaluation quickly becomes impractical as $n_C$ increases.

For example, a cluster containing only $20$ observations already admits

$$
2^{19}-1
=
524{,}287
$$

distinct non-trivial binary splits.

Divisive procedures therefore require a practical rule for constructing a useful split without exhaustively evaluating every possible bipartition.

## A Dissimilarity-Based Divisive Procedure

One such procedure constructs a split directly from pairwise dissimilarities.

Suppose a cluster $G$ is to be divided. Initially, all of its observations belong to $G$, while a second cluster $H$ is empty.

The first step identifies the observation having the largest average dissimilarity from the other observations in $G$.

For observation $i\in G$, define

$$
a(i,G)
=
\frac{1}{|G|-1}
\sum_{\substack{j\in G\\j\neq i}}
d_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-divisive-average-dissimilarity}

The initial observation transferred from $G$ to $H$ is

$$
i^\ast
=
\underset{i\in G}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}
\;
a(i,G).
$$ {#eq-divisive-initial-object}

This observation is, on average, the most dissimilar from the rest of the current cluster. It becomes the first member of the new group:

$$
H=\{i^\ast\}.
$$

The original group is correspondingly reduced to

$$
G
\leftarrow
G\setminus\{i^\ast\}.
$$

The procedure must now determine whether additional observations should move from $G$ to $H$.

For each remaining observation $i\in G$, compare its average dissimilarity from the observations currently in $H$ with its average dissimilarity from the other observations remaining in $G$.

Define

$$
a(i,H)
=
\frac{1}{|H|}
\sum_{j\in H}
d_{ij},
$$ {#eq-divisive-dissimilarity-to-h}

and, provided $|G|>1$,

$$
a(i,G\setminus\{i\})
=
\frac{1}{|G|-1}
\sum_{\substack{j\in G\\j\neq i}}
d_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-divisive-dissimilarity-to-g}

The difference

$$
\delta_i
=
a(i,G\setminus\{i\})
-
a(i,H)
$$ {#eq-divisive-transfer-score}

measures whether observation $i$ is, on average, more dissimilar from the observations remaining in $G$ than from those already transferred to $H$.

If

$$
\delta_i>0,
$$

then

$$
a(i,H)
<
a(i,G\setminus\{i\}),
$$

so observation $i$ is closer on average to the emerging group $H$ than to the observations remaining in $G$.

The next observation selected for transfer is therefore

$$
i^\ast
=
\underset{i\in G}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}
\;
\delta_i.
$$ {#eq-divisive-transfer-rule}

If the largest value satisfies

$$
\delta_{i^\ast}>0,
$$

the observation is moved:

$$
H
\leftarrow
H\cup\{i^\ast\},
$$

$$
G
\leftarrow
G\setminus\{i^\ast\}.
$$

The average dissimilarities are then recomputed and the process is repeated.

When

$$
\max_{i\in G}\delta_i<0,
$$ {#eq-divisive-stopping-rule}

no remaining observation is, on average, closer to $H$ than to the other observations in $G$. The transfer process stops, producing the binary split

$$
C
=
G\cup H.
$$ {#eq-divisive-resulting-split}

This provides a constructive alternative to evaluating all $2^{n_C-1}-1$ possible binary partitions.

## A Small Example

Consider a cluster containing four observations with dissimilarity matrix

$$
\mathbf{D}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 7 & 8 \\
1 & 0 & 6 & 7 \\
7 & 6 & 0 & 2 \\
8 & 7 & 2 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-divisive-example-matrix}

Initially,

$$
G=\{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

The average dissimilarity of observation $1$ from the others is

$$
a(1,G)
=
\frac{1+7+8}{3}
=
\frac{16}{3}.
$$

For observation $2$,

$$
a(2,G)
=
\frac{1+6+7}{3}
=
\frac{14}{3}.
$$

For observation $3$,

$$
a(3,G)
=
\frac{7+6+2}{3}
=
5.
$$

For observation $4$,

$$
a(4,G)
=
\frac{8+7+2}{3}
=
\frac{17}{3}.
$$

Since

$$
\frac{17}{3}
>
\frac{16}{3}
>
5
>
\frac{14}{3},
$$

observation $4$ has the largest average dissimilarity and becomes the first member of $H$:

$$
H=\{4\},
\qquad
G=\{1,2,3\}.
$$

Now consider observation $3$. Its average dissimilarity from the other observations remaining in $G$ is

$$
a(3,G\setminus\{3\})
=
\frac{7+6}{2}
=
6.5,
$$

while its average dissimilarity from $H$ is

$$
a(3,H)
=
2.
$$

Hence,

$$
\delta_3
=
6.5-2
=
4.5.
$$

Observation $3$ is therefore substantially closer to the emerging group $H$ than to observations $1$ and $2$ remaining in $G$, so it is transferred:

$$
H=\{3,4\},
\qquad
G=\{1,2\}.
$$

Now consider observation $1$. Its average dissimilarity from the other member of $G$ is

$$
a(1,G\setminus\{1\})
=
1,
$$

while its average dissimilarity from $H$ is

$$
a(1,H)
=
\frac{7+8}{2}
=
7.5.
$$

Thus,

$$
\delta_1
=
1-7.5
=
-6.5.
$$

Similarly, for observation $2$,

$$
a(2,G\setminus\{2\})
=
1,
$$

and

$$
a(2,H)
=
\frac{6+7}{2}
=
6.5,
$$

giving

$$
\delta_2
=
1-6.5
=
-5.5.
$$

Since neither transfer score is positive, the splitting procedure stops. The resulting division is

$$
\{1,2\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\{3,4\}.
$$

The example illustrates the top-down logic clearly. The procedure first identifies an observation that is poorly integrated with the original group and then allows other observations to join the emerging daughter cluster when their average dissimilarities support doing so.

## Recursive Splitting

A single binary split produces two daughter clusters, but a complete hierarchy requires the procedure to continue recursively.

Starting from

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(1)}
=
\{\mathcal{S}\},
$$

the first split produces

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(2)}
=
\{C_1,C_2\}.
$$

One of these clusters is subsequently selected for another split, producing

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(3)}
=
\{C_{11},C_{12},C_2\},
$$

or alternatively

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(3)}
=
\{C_1,C_{21},C_{22}\}.
$$

The procedure continues until the desired resolution is reached or, for a complete hierarchy, until every terminal cluster contains one observation.

The divisive approach can therefore be particularly attractive when the main interest lies near the top of the hierarchy. If only a small number of broad groups is required, the algorithm can focus directly on the large-scale divisions without first constructing all of the fine-scale agglomerations near the leaves.

## Divisive Procedures Based on Other Clustering Methods

The top-down paradigm does not require every split to be constructed from the particular dissimilarity-based procedure above.

A binary partitioning method can instead be applied recursively. For example, a cluster can be divided by applying $K$-means with

$$
K=2,
$$

and then applying the same procedure recursively to selected daughter clusters.

Similarly, a $K$-medoids procedure with

$$
K=2
$$

can be used to construct successive splits.

These approaches illustrate an important distinction: *divisive hierarchical clustering* describes the direction and nested structure of the procedure, while the rule used to construct each binary split can vary.

There are, however, consequences to this flexibility. If the splitting method depends on an initial configuration, as $K$-means typically does, the resulting hierarchy can inherit that dependence. Moreover, an arbitrary sequence of recursive binary partitions does not automatically guarantee monotone dendrogram levels.

Thus, constructing nested partitions is not by itself sufficient to reproduce every property associated with the agglomerative dendrograms considered earlier.

## Agglomerative and Divisive Views

The two paradigms can be summarized schematically as

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ccc}
\text{Agglomerative}
&
:
&
\text{local groups}
\longrightarrow
\text{global structure}
\\[4pt]
\text{Divisive}
&
:
&
\text{global structure}
\longrightarrow
\text{local groups}
\end{array}
}
$$

Agglomerative clustering makes its earliest decisions among individual observations or small clusters. Those decisions become irreversible components of progressively larger groups.

Divisive clustering makes its earliest decisions at the level of the complete dataset or large clusters. Those decisions determine the broad branches within which subsequent finer divisions must occur.

Neither direction removes the hierarchical constraint. In both cases, once the tree has been constructed, partitions at different levels are nested.

The distinction is therefore not between hierarchical and non-hierarchical clustering, but between two ways of constructing the same general type of nested representation.

# Applications and Extensions

Hierarchical clustering is useful when the objective is not only to assign observations to groups, but also to understand relationships among those groups at different levels of resolution.

This distinguishes it from methods that return a single partition. A hierarchical analysis retains information about how local groups combine into broader structures, making it particularly useful when the data may contain nested organization or when the appropriate number of clusters is not known in advance.

The method is therefore best understood not as belonging to one particular application domain, but as a general framework for organizing objects from pairwise relationships.

## Exploratory Structure Discovery

One of the most direct applications of hierarchical clustering is exploratory data analysis.

Suppose a dataset contains observations

$$
\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_N
$$

but no response variable and no known group labels. A hierarchical analysis can be used to investigate whether the observations exhibit organization at several scales.

For example, a dendrogram may reveal that

$$
\{1,2,3\}
$$

forms a relatively tight group, while

$$
\{4,5\}
$$

forms another. At a higher level, these two groups may themselves merge before joining the remaining observations.

The resulting structure contains more information than the statement that the data contain, say, three clusters. It describes relationships among clusters as well as membership within them.

This is particularly useful when several levels of aggregation have substantive meaning. A coarse partition may identify broad families of observations, while lower levels reveal subdivisions within those families.

As discussed earlier, these patterns should not automatically be interpreted as intrinsic structure in the population. The hierarchy remains conditional on the representation of the observations, the dissimilarity measure, and the clustering criterion.

## Two-Way Organization of Data Matrices

A particularly useful application arises when both the rows and columns of a data matrix represent objects that can meaningfully be grouped.

Consider

$$
\mathbf{X}
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}.
$$

Ordinarily, clustering is applied to the rows,

$$
\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_N,
$$

producing a hierarchy among the $N$ observations.

But the columns can also be treated as objects. Writing

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}^{(1)}
&
\mathbf{x}^{(2)}
&
\cdots
&
\mathbf{x}^{(p)}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}^{(j)}$ denotes the $j$th column, hierarchical clustering can be applied independently to

$$
\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{x}^{(p)}.
$$

This produces two hierarchies:

$$
\text{row hierarchy}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\text{column hierarchy}.
$$

The rows and columns of $\mathbf{X}$ can then be reordered according to these structures.

A well-known example occurs with gene-expression data. The rows of the matrix may represent genes and the columns biological samples. Clustering the genes groups together similar expression profiles, while clustering the samples groups together observations with similar patterns across genes.

The reordered matrix can then be displayed as a heatmap accompanied by two dendrograms.

![Schematic representation of two-way hierarchical clustering. Rows and columns of a data matrix are clustered independently and reordered according to their respective dendrograms, exposing block structure that may be difficult to identify in the original ordering.](figures/two-way-hierarchical-clustering.png){#fig-two-way-hierarchical-clustering}

The purpose of the rearrangement in @fig-two-way-hierarchical-clustering is not to change the values in the matrix. It changes only their ordering.

If $\mathbf{P}_r$ and $\mathbf{P}_c$ denote permutation matrices determined from the row and column hierarchies, respectively, the reordered matrix can be written as

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}
=
\mathbf{P}_r
\mathbf{X}
\mathbf{P}_c^\top.
$$ {#eq-two-way-reordered-matrix}

No observations or variables have been added or removed. The transformation exposes structure by placing similar rows and columns near one another.

This is a useful example of hierarchical clustering serving simultaneously as an analytical and visualization tool.

## Information Organization

Hierarchical clustering can also be applied when the objects are not naturally interpreted as points in a low-dimensional Euclidean space.

The essential input to many hierarchical methods is a dissimilarity matrix,

$$
\mathbf{D}
=
[d_{ij}],
$$

rather than a particular coordinate representation.

This makes the framework applicable whenever meaningful pairwise similarities or dissimilarities can be constructed.

Documents, for example, can be represented through measures of similarity derived from their content. A hierarchy can then organize closely related documents into local groups and those groups into broader collections.

The same general principle applies to other collections of objects for which pairwise relationships are more natural than a predefined set of numerical coordinates.

This was already implicit in the original formulation of hierarchical clustering developed in these notes: once an appropriate dissimilarity matrix has been constructed, the clustering procedure operates on relationships among objects rather than on the semantic meaning of the objects themselves.

## Hierarchical Model-Based Clustering

The classical procedures considered so far are based primarily on dissimilarities and deterministic merging or splitting rules. Hierarchical structure can also be combined with explicit statistical models.

Suppose observations within a cluster are represented by a probability model

$$
p(\mathbf{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}_k),
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\theta}_k$ denotes the parameters associated with cluster $k$.

A mixture model instead represents the overall distribution as

$$
p(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\pi_k
p(\mathbf{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}_k),
$$ {#eq-mixture-model}

where

$$
\pi_k\geq0
$$

and

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k=1.
$$

Hierarchical model-based approaches organize such local probabilistic models within a tree. Rather than defining a cluster only through pairwise dissimilarities, the groups can therefore be associated with fitted probability distributions.

This changes the statistical interpretation of the clustering problem. Classical agglomerative hierarchical clustering asks which groups should be combined according to a linkage criterion. A model-based hierarchy can instead ask how the data should be recursively represented by probabilistic components.

Model-selection criteria can then enter the construction of the hierarchy. For example, information criteria such as AIC or BIC may be used to compare candidate statistical representations.

These methods should not be confused with Ward's method. Ward's criterion is based on the increase in within-cluster squared dispersion,

$$
\Delta(A,B)
=
\frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}
\left\|
\boldsymbol{\mu}_A-\boldsymbol{\mu}_B
\right\|_2^2,
$$

but it does not specify a probability distribution for the observations. A model-based hierarchy introduces an explicit probabilistic assumption.

## Hierarchical Representations Beyond Classical Linkage

The idea of organizing observations at multiple levels extends beyond the classical linkage methods.

Hierarchical self-organizing maps provide one example. Self-organizing maps construct structured low-dimensional representations of data, and hierarchical variants organize these representations across multiple levels.

Other approaches combine hierarchical organization with graph-based or spectral ideas. In these settings, relationships among observations may be represented through an adjacency structure rather than only through the conventional Euclidean geometry used by methods such as Ward's criterion.

These approaches share the idea of multilevel organization but should not all be regarded as interchangeable versions of classical agglomerative clustering. Their objectives, representations, and algorithms can be substantially different.

The connection is conceptual:

$$
\boxed{
\text{complex collection of observations}
\longrightarrow
\text{nested or multilevel representation}
}
$$

rather than a claim that all hierarchical methods optimize the same criterion.

## Large-Scale Hierarchical Clustering

The $O(N^2)$ computational and storage requirements encountered in classical hierarchical clustering become important when $N$ is large.

This has motivated approaches that change the representation of the clustering problem.

One possibility is to partition the data space into cells and operate on those cells rather than repeatedly comparing every pair of individual observations. Grid-based methods follow this general strategy.

Let the observation space be partitioned into cells

$$
G_1,G_2,\ldots,G_M.
$$

Each cell can be summarized by quantities such as its occupancy or density,

$$
\rho_m
=
\#\{\mathbf{x}_i:\mathbf{x}_i\in G_m\}.
$$ {#eq-grid-cell-density}

The clustering problem can then be expressed partly in terms of relationships among cells rather than exclusively among the original $N$ observations.

Density-based approaches make a related change in perspective. Instead of defining clusters solely through pairwise proximity or centroid dispersion, they identify regions containing relatively high concentrations of observations separated by regions of lower density.

These approaches address problems that classical hierarchical clustering does not solve automatically, including scalability, noise, and clusters with more complicated geometric shapes.

They are therefore better regarded as extensions of the broader clustering landscape than as minor modifications of a linkage coefficient.

## Multiscale Structure

One recurring idea across hierarchical methods is *scale*.

A partition with many clusters describes fine structure. A partition with fewer clusters describes progressively coarser structure. Classical hierarchical clustering expresses this through nested partitions,

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(N)}
\preceq
\mathcal{P}^{(N-1)}
\preceq
\cdots
\preceq
\mathcal{P}^{(1)}.
$$

Other multiscale methods achieve related objectives through different mathematical mechanisms.

For example, grid-based methods can vary the spatial resolution at which observations are aggregated. Transform-based approaches can separate structure according to scale before groups are identified. Model-based methods can place local distributions inside progressively broader probabilistic structures.

The common idea is not a particular linkage criterion but the representation of structure at more than one level of resolution.

This is one reason hierarchical ideas appear across otherwise different clustering methodologies.

## When Hierarchical Clustering Is Useful

The classical hierarchical framework is particularly useful when the nested structure itself carries information.

It is well suited to situations in which:

- relationships among clusters are as important as the final cluster assignments;
- several levels of resolution may be meaningful;
- an informative dissimilarity between observations can be defined;
- visual inspection of the organization through a dendrogram is useful;
- the dataset is sufficiently small for the computational requirements to remain manageable.

Conversely, hierarchical clustering may be less attractive when the principal objective is only to obtain one partition of a very large dataset, when the expected groupings at different values of $K$ are not naturally nested, or when the chosen dissimilarity and linkage criterion do not correspond well to the structure of interest.

The method should therefore be selected because the hierarchical representation is useful for the problem, not merely because a dendrogram can be produced.

# Summary

Hierarchical clustering constructs a nested representation of observations from a chosen notion of dissimilarity. Unlike clustering methods that return only a single partition, it describes how groups are related across multiple levels of resolution.

The starting point is a set of observations,

$$
\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_N,
$$

together with pairwise dissimilarities

$$
d_{ij}
=
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j).
$$

These values define the relationships among individual observations. A linkage criterion extends this notion from observations to clusters,

$$
d_{ij}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
d_L(A,B),
$$

and therefore determines how the hierarchy is constructed.

In agglomerative hierarchical clustering, the procedure begins with

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(N)}
=
\big\{
\{1\},\{2\},\ldots,\{N\}
\big\}
$$

and repeatedly merges the pair of clusters selected by

$$
(A,B)
=
\underset{C_r\neq C_s}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}
\;
d_L(C_r,C_s).
$$

After exactly $N-1$ mergers, all observations belong to a single cluster.

Different linkage criteria encode different definitions of inter-cluster similarity. Single linkage depends on the closest pair of observations, complete linkage on the most distant pair, average linkage on the average cross-cluster dissimilarity, and centroid linkage on the separation between cluster centroids. Ward's method takes a different but related perspective, selecting the merge that produces the smallest increase in within-cluster dispersion:

$$
\Delta(A,B)
=
\frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}
\left\|
\boldsymbol{\mu}_A-\boldsymbol{\mu}_B
\right\|_2^2.
$$

Many of these methods can be expressed through the Lance--Williams recurrence,

$$
d(A\cup B,C)
=
\alpha_A d(A,C)
+
\alpha_B d(B,C)
+
\beta d(A,B)
+
\gamma
\left|
d(A,C)-d(B,C)
\right|,
$$

which separates the clustering criterion from the mechanism used to update inter-cluster dissimilarities.

The hierarchy can be represented through a dendrogram. For monotone methods, the height at which two branches join records the dissimilarity associated with their merger. This induces a cophenetic dissimilarity between every pair of observations and connects hierarchical clustering with ultrametric structure.

A horizontal cut through the dendrogram converts the hierarchy into a conventional partition. Different cuts produce different numbers of clusters while preserving the nesting property:

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(N)}
\preceq
\mathcal{P}^{(N-1)}
\preceq
\cdots
\preceq
\mathcal{P}^{(1)}.
$$

This nested structure is both a defining feature and a restriction. Useful partitions at different levels need not be hierarchically compatible, and the existence of a dendrogram does not establish that the underlying data possess a natural hierarchy.

The computational implementation is also distinct from the clustering criterion itself. A direct agglomerative implementation that repeatedly searches all active cluster pairs can require

$$
O(N^3)
$$

time, while the complete pairwise dissimilarity representation requires

$$
O(N^2)
$$

storage. Lance--Williams updates and nearest-neighbor-based algorithms can substantially improve the construction of the hierarchy for suitable linkage criteria.

Hierarchical clustering can alternatively proceed in the opposite direction. Divisive methods begin with the complete dataset and recursively split existing clusters,

$$
1
\longrightarrow
2
\longrightarrow
\cdots
\longrightarrow
N,
$$

rather than building the hierarchy from singleton observations upward. Agglomerative and divisive methods therefore construct the same general type of nested representation from opposite directions.

The complete analysis can be summarized as

$$
\boxed{
\text{data}
\longrightarrow
\text{dissimilarity}
\longrightarrow
\text{clustering criterion}
\longrightarrow
\text{hierarchy}
\longrightarrow
\text{interpretation}
}
$$

Each step matters. The data representation determines which differences are visible, the dissimilarity defines what it means for observations to be close, the clustering criterion determines how those relationships are propagated from observations to groups, and the resulting hierarchy must finally be interpreted in the context of the problem.

For this reason, hierarchical clustering should not be viewed simply as an algorithm for producing a dendrogram. It is a framework for representing multilevel structure under explicit assumptions about similarity and group formation. Its value lies not only in obtaining clusters, but in making the relationships among those clusters available for analysis.
